editorials.title: A nation’s song: On Vande Mataram’s rendition
editorials.passage:
Patriotism is not just reverence for a territory or a flag but is the embodiment of solidarity with fellow citizens in a nation-state. The idea of a nation as a bond transcends family, community or faith, uniting citizens through common values and a pursuit of prosperity. National symbols and anthems exist to hone that bond. When they are changed or modified to compel citizens to accept a majoritarian version, their purpose is defeated. India’s freedom fighting generation understood this. Which is why, in 1937, the Congress Working Committee resolved that only the first two stanzas of Bankim Chatterjee’s Vande Mataram should be sung at national gatherings, since the later stanzas invoke the motherland as Hindu deities. When Jana Gana Mana was adopted as the National Anthem on January 24, 1950, India’s first President Rajendra Prasad said that Vande Mataram, even though there is no mention of a “national song” in the Constitution, would be “honoured equally”. Since then, the two-stanza version has allowed citizens of all faiths to partake in a song that stirred the freedom struggle and popularised by artistes such as Lata Mangeshkar and A.R. Rahman.

In the last year or so, the BJP-led Union government has sought to unsettle this inclusive compact. Since the song’s 150th anniversary in 2025, it has pushed for all six stanzas to be recited. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) issued directions and circulars in 2026 and Parliament passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026 with little debate — actions that are in line with the BJP’s habit of imposing uniformity and majoritarian preference on all citizens. The amendment extends Section 3 of the 1971 Act, which punishes anyone who intentionally prevents the singing of the National Anthem or disturbs an assembly engaged in such singing, to the National Song. Per se it does not compel anyone to sing or define the National Song or its stanzas. But read alongside the MHA orders, which prescribe an official version of all six stanzas, mandate mass singing at public functions, and place the song before the anthem, it amounts to compulsion, as a petition by T.M. Krishna in the Supreme Court has argued. The Court has rightly observed that the state may decide what the National Song is, but cannot penalise conscientious objectors in line with Bijoe Emmanuel (1986). This judgment held that no law obliges anyone to sing the Anthem, standing in respectful silence is no offence and executive instructions without statutory backing cannot curtail fundamental rights. The Court must apply Bijoe Emmanuel in full, set aside the MHA’s orders and make it clear that silence cannot be read as “disturbance”. By reverting to the vision of the freedom generation, the Court will do justice to the idea of unity in diversity.

editorials.title: A chance to retreat: On Donald Trump, the Greenland agreement
editorials.passage:
President Donald Trump first raised the possibility of acquiring Greenland, a Danish territory, during his first term in office. After his return to the White House in January 2025, he doubled down on his threat, saying that he would make the island American territory one way or the other. This incensed Denmark, a founding member of NATO, as well as America’s other allies in Europe. Denmark reasserted its sovereignty over the island but, as a compromise, promised to let the U.S. expand its military presence. On September 22, the leaders of the U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed a new security deal , which, according to Mr. Trump, would allow the U.S. to do “what is necessary in Greenland”. For Mr. Trump, who had even raised the possibility of using force to take over the territory, the deal is a retreat from his acquisition demand. But at the same time, it re-endorses the U.S. role as the primary security provider — it already stations some 150 troops in Greenland at its Pituffik Space Base. Under the agreement, Washington would build military facilities in Narsarsuaq in the south, where the U.S. had an airfield during the Second World War, and in Mestersvig in the east, along the Norwegian Sea.

The 1951 U.S.-Denmark security agreement provides Washington the broad rights to build military bases in the ice-covered island. During the Second World War and the Cold War, the U.S. had more than 30 bases and installations on the island. Most were shut down over the years, particularly after the Cold War. In recent years, Trump administration officials raised concerns about the growing activities of China and Russia in the Arctic, including alleged espionage. As the Arctic region’s strategic profile is rising — partly because melting ice opens up previously impassable regions — the U.S. wants to consolidate its position and believes that Greenland would play a key role in that strategy. The agreement says that even if Greenland, which has a population of around 50,000, becomes independent, it would respect the deal with the U.S. and stay in NATO. In other words, this provides the U.S. indefinite access to the island’s military facilities. The deal also stipulates that no hostile power (non-NATO countries) can establish military facilities in Greenland or invest in its sensitive areas (mainly rare earths). Denmark has already blocked Chinese investments in the territory and the deal effectively formalises that restriction. So, on paper, Greenland could remain a self-governing, autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, while the U.S. would be its strategic patron with greater control — a diplomatic arrangement acceptable to Washington, NATO and Denmark.

editorials.title: Apart from culprits, act against assault videos shared online
editorials.passage: Women and girls are accustomed to having their movements restricted in the name of safety. If they venture out alone and face violence, society often turns the accusatory lens on them to police their behaviour, rather than the perpetrator. Taking a male relative or friend along is thought to protect them. Yet, recent incidents in a New Delhi park and two Bihar districts have shown that even such a safeguard can be meaningless. On the contrary, the presence of a boy with a young girl is easily weaponised against her on the euphemism of ‘moral policing’. In reality, this behaviour that is often exercised by men—and validated by other men—is another way in which patriarchal values are reinforced by clamping down on women’s rights and freedoms.In the Delhi case, three men are accused of sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl, who was accompanied by a male friend, by posing as police personnel. In Bihar’s Jamui, the violence that a girl and her teenage classmates faced after sundown was filmed. Just days later, another video from Samastipur was shared in which a group rounds up on a young couple in broad daylight..Following these incidents, women students of the renowned Lady Shri Ram College in Delhi, that is located near the park, raised concerns for their own safety. Meanwhile, Bihar police initiated action to take down videos of the underage girls’ molestation from social media accounts.Three aspects deserve particular attention. First, almost 14 years after the Delhi rape protests, it is unconscionable that public spaces in the capital and elsewhere remain utterly unsafe for women. The ‘smartness’ of India’s cities is meaningless if they cannot, at the very least, be well-lit and adequately policed. Second, filming of sexual violence by perpetrators has become a dangerous norm. In such cases, the police must also invoke the relevant laws to crack down on the additional digital violence that re-victimises the survivor for as long as the material is online. Policymakers must also examine if the existing laws suffice to target the evolving methods of sexual violence in the digital sphere, especially if visuals are shared in the seedier sections of mainstream platforms for profit. editorials.title: MLA disqualification puts glare on other defectors
editorials.passage: Telangana is headed for yet another bypoll with the Supreme Court on Thursday upholding the high court order disqualifying former MLA Danam Nagender under the anti-defection law. The ruling has once again brought to the fore the vexed question of defection and the Speaker’s role in deciding its consequence.Nagender won at the last Assembly elections on a BRS ticket and soon walked over to the ruling Congress. He then contested the Lok Sabha polls on a Congress ticket. Apart from him, nine others had also defected to the Congress from the BRS. After repeated raps from the judiciary for delays, Speaker Gaddam Prasad Kumar dismissed disqualification pleas against all of them, reasoning there was no substantive evidence against the legislators.However, the high court found the Speaker’s decision on Nagender to be in violation of Article 191(2) and the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution. The Supreme Court rightly upheld the verdict, for it is obvious that by contesting on a Congress ticket, Nagender had given up his membership of the opposition party. The development forces us to seriously reconsider whether to let the Speaker function as a quasi-judicial tribunal or have a separate impartial body to adjudicate on defections..Parliament must deliberate on this crucial issue because defections are rising every year, repeatedly betraying the people’s mandate. It is nothing short of a mockery of democracy. It must be noted that almost all political parties—including the BRS—are guilty of poaching legislators and undermining the anti-defection law.In the Telangana case, the defecting legislators did take part in Congress activities one way or another. But as their numbers fall well short of two-thirds of the BRS legislature party, they attract the anti-defection law. Since the Speaker has dismissed pleas against them, the ball is in the court. The question now is whether the other turncoats, too, will face disqualification.The political fallout of the top court’s ruling cannot be exaggerated. A bypoll, that too in Hyderabad, will be an acid test for the Congress with the BRS and BJP trying their best to deliver a blow. With the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation elections also due, the Congress can ill afford to lose. Whoever wins, the sticking point is that an avoidable election has been thrust upon the people..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Driven to work
editorials.passage: At a time Gen Z and Millennial workers are demanding better work-life balance, more employees are feeling less connected to jobs. Gallup’s latest global workplace survey, with views from 263,810 respondents worldwide collected through 2025, found that falling engagement among managers resulted in a slump in overall employee engagement. Whereas the global average of engaged workers was at 30 percent, Indians registered at only 23 percent, with the share falling for the fourth straight year. The most populous nation is so job-starved that the demand for any livelihood obscures the quest for quality work. The debate must also consider job satisfaction, because a sharp slump there would also be reflected as a societal crisis..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: 22 languages, score 0
editorials.passage:
Point a state-of-the-art language model at the names of the Northeast ~ Khasi surnames, Garo festivals, the titles a clan carries ~ and ask it to recognise them, and it returns a number that should stop a clearance meeting: an F1 score of zero. Not low. Zero. The finding is not a complaint on a blog; it sits in this year’s record of the Association for Computational Linguistics, where a researcher from Shillong, Badal Nyalang, showed two failures that compound ~ the model cannot see the culturally freighted name at all, and the tokeniser beneath it mangles the diacritics that carry meaning in Khasi and the morpheme mark that holds Garo together, corrupting them in up to half the cases across the models tested. 

A purpose-built regional tagger, made on the community’s own terms, scored 0.964 on the same ground. The gap between zero and that is not compute. It is attention. This is the hole in India’s sovereign-AI story: it keeps a language count and no civilisation ledger. The country has decided, rightly, to build its own models rather than rent them from California, and put real money and hardware behind the decision. But a foundation model is only as sovereign as the meanings beneath it, and a model can be taught to produce fluent Khasi while remaining blind to the people who live inside the language. India is measuring breadth ~ how many tongues, how many datasets, how many chips ~ and calling it depth. 

The build itself is serious, and its architects deserve to be heard fairly. Under the IndiaAI Mission, a common compute pool of tens of thousands of subsidised processors has been assembled where two years ago there was almost none, within reach of a start-up in Pune or a lab in Guwahati. From more than 500 applications the government has chosen twenty indigenous model proposals to fund. BharatGen, the IIT Bombay-led consortium at the centre of the effort, has released Param2, a seventeen-billion-parameter model it says now generates text across all twenty-two scheduled languages ~ the constitutional list it was asked to reach. 

For years the world’s models treated Indian languages as a rounding error; a scheduled-language list on a state-backed model is a political fact before a technical one, and worth having. None of this is the error. The error is in mistaking the menu for the meal. A parameter is a dial the model turns as it reads, and seventeen billion of them can emit grammatical sentences on a surprisingly thin diet of a language. What the model has actually digested is the harder question, and the answer is uneven in ways a coverage badge cannot show. 

Machine-readable text is overwhelmingly recent, urban, written and argumentative; the oral, the liturgical, the dialectal and the manuscript are thin on the ground. A model fed mostly on that diet will render a Bhojpuri or a Meitei sentence fluently and hollowly ~ right in the words, deaf to the register, confident in precisely the places a native speaker would pause. The engineers have an answer, and it is a fair one. Modern models do not learn each language from a blank slate; they transfer, carrying structure from data-rich languages into data-poor ones, so a little Khasi now travels further than it once did. Coverage first, the argument runs; depth follows the corpora grow. 

There is truth in it. But transfer borrows the shape of the languages it already knows, and a model that reaches Khasi through the scaffolding of English and Hindi inherits their blind spots ~ which is precisely how a system ends up scoring zero on the names a community holds dearest while producing paragraphs that look, to anyone who cannot check, entirely fluent. The languages that most need representation are the ones transfer serves worst, because there is least of them to correct the borrowed guess. Fluency is not fidelity, and a mission built to close a gap can, mistaking one for the other, reopen it in a costlier and less visible form. 

The state is not blind to this. AIKosh, the national data platform, is the right instrument ~ a public shelf where datasets in Indian languages can be pooled and reused rather than rebuilt behind every team’s walls. It has grown ferociously, from a few hundred datasets at its launch last year to more than 15,000 now. But a count is not a corpus. Much of what fills that shelf is ministry operational data; the annotated cultural and linguistic material a low-resource language actually needs ~ the transcribed speech, the named-entity set a Khasi scholar has checked by hand ~ is the slow, unglamorous part, and it does not accumulate at the speed of a dashboard. The compute pillar is counted in thousands of crore; the labour of building that deeper record commands nothing like the same purse or urgency. 

There is a further reason that record cannot simply be hurried. A language is not an ownerless commodity lying about to be scraped; it is the property, in every sense but the legal one, of the people who speak it. To assemble a Santali or a Tulu corpus at national scale is to decide whose recordings are taken, on what terms, and to whose benefit the model trained on them is put ~ questions of consent and ownership that a processor order never raises. Nyalang’s regional tagger worked because it was built with the community whose names it had to recognise, not merely at them. 

Gather the material carelessly and the result is a new extraction dressed as inclusion; gather it well and the corpus becomes a public asset with a public warrant behind it. Either way the work is governance, not procurement, and governance keeps no quarterly schedule. This is the quiet miscalculation beneath a sound decision. What cannot be added up cannot be governed, and the mission has built a system engineered to add up languages and never to add up distortions. 

The remedy need not be exotic. Give every publicly funded model a scorecard by language and region ~ a running ledger, not a marketing badge ~ disclosing where it is fluent and where blind, tested before launch by linguists and community scholars rather than by the builders alone, with a public channel through which a tracked error on a name, a festival or a sacred term is filed and fixed. India already runs tougher disclosure regimes on its banks and its environmental clearances; a model that will soon answer a farmer in Marathi, or a patient in a register no English corpus has seen, deserves no lighter a standard. India has resolved, rightly, to make the century’s most strategic technology at home and in its own languages, and the resolve is worth the money behind it. 

But intelligence in a language is not conjured out of silicon; it is distilled from what a people have written, recorded and been willing to share, and checked by someone who can tell a clan-name from a place-name. The models will speak all 22 languages soon enough. The question the mission’s ledgers do not yet put is the only one the speech communities will finally answer for themselves: understood by whom ~ and for the meanings the machine has flattened, from where? 

The writers are, respectively, a practising Chartered Accountant and a practising Company Secretary. They can be reached at kannan@cakt.in and csshaliniiyengar@gmail.com)

editorials.title: Clean air needed for climate action
editorials.passage:
The BRICS Summit in New Delhi ended with a declaration that reflects the difficult energy choices facing emerging economies. It calls for a just and equitable energy transition, presses for greater climate finance and access to technology, and acknowledges that fossil fuels will continue to have a place in the energy mix of developing countries. It also reaffirms the Paris Agreement and argues that national circumstances must shape the route countries take towards lower emissions. There is, however, a curious absence. 

For all its attention to climate, energy and sustainable development, the declaration does not explicitly address one of the most immediate environmental costs borne by many BRICS economies: air pollution. Many BRICS countries are trying to solve two problems at once. They need more energy, transport and industrial production as incomes rise, while the health and economic costs of the way that growth is powered are becoming harder to ignore. In South Asia, the numbers are particularly difficult to dismiss. A new assessment by the UN Environment Programme and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition estimates that air pollution already imposes an economic burden equivalent to about 10 per cent of South Asia’s GDP, the highest of any region assessed. 

The study also calculates that a package of measures tackling air pollution and climate change together could return around Rs 21 in economic and health benefits for every Rs 1 invested in South Asia. The benefit-cost ratio is the second highest among the 15 regions UNEP examined. This does not mean that a government spends one rupee and gets Rs 21 back. The return comes from losses avoided: lower healthcare costs, fewer missed workdays, higher productivity and less physical damage, alongside harder-to-price gains from avoided illness and premature death. 

Even excluding those non-market benefits, UNEP finds that measurable market returns at the global level still amount to about four dollars for every dollar spent. That strengthens the case for early action in developing economies, where governments are decarbonising while still building power systems, cities and industries. Cleaner air delivers benefits now, while climate gains accumulate over time. Cleaner buses, household fuels, industrial standards and power systems can reduce emissions while improving air quality. UNEP finds that the air-pollution gains are felt early, while the economic benefits from avoided climate damage build over decades. For governments with limited fiscal space, that timing matters. 

Energy transformation across power, industry and households is therefore especially relevant to the BRICS debate. By 2035, clean cooking and heating offers the largest return among the measures examined for South Asia, followed by the transformation of power generation and industrial process emission standards. By 2050, industrial process standards, vehicle emission standards and power-sector transformation move ahead. India has experience of what such transitions look like when taken to scale. The expansion of LPG access under the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana changed household energy use across millions of homes. The growth of solar power changed the scale and economics of renewable-energy deployment. UNEP itself cites India’s clean-cooking programme and solar mission as examples of policies that have driven technological and social change. But India’s next set of choices will have to be more local. 

Pollution profiles differ sharply from one state to another, and within states. What makes sense in an industrial district may be quite different from what is needed in an agricultural belt, a large city or a Himalayan state. National policy can set standards and provide finance; the choice of what to tackle first will often have to be made at the subnational level. Some states have begun moving in this direction. Punjab has examined non-CO2 pollutants alongside its longer-term climate pathway, bringing methane, black carbon and ozone into a debate that has often centred on carbon dioxide. 

Haryana faces a related mix of agricultural, transport and urban sources within the wider Indo-Gangetic airshed. In Himalayan states such as Himachal Pradesh, warming and air pollution play out against fragile ecosystems and different patterns of energy use, transport and development. Madhya Pradesh offers a particularly useful example of how granular this exercise needs to be. Indore, Bhopal and Jabalpur have performed strongly in recent Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan rankings. But the state's pollution challenge extends well beyond its better-performing cities. 

Its recent Non-CO2 Emission Reduction Pathways for Madhya Pradesh maps emissions across all 55 districts, identifying where livestock, industry, power generation, transport and other sources dominate. The learning is that a state should not spend the same rupee in the same way everywhere. Industrial areas may need cleaner fuels and tighter emission standards; elsewhere, the priorities may be transport, household energy, agriculture or waste. That variation also makes coordination harder. The levers span transport, municipal administration, power, agriculture, petroleum and pollution-control agencies, while the pollution is omnipresent.

 Across the measures examined by UNEP, average implementation delays are estimated at roughly 7.5 to eight years. Institutional barriers are the largest single contributor, ahead of technical, economic and so cial constraints. Weak coordination, limited enforcement capacity and fragmented decision-making can turn policies already available on paper into benefits that arrive years late. Achieving national air- quality standards on schedule from 2026 is estimated to reduce cumulative PM2.5 exposure by about 20 per cent by 2040. Introduce an eight-year delay and the reduction falls to 10 per cent. Half the gain disappears. A pollution-control system installed years late cannot clean the air people have already breathed. Cleaner buses purchased in the next decade cannot restore school days and working days already lost. 

Later action cannot undo illnesses that develop while implementation stalled. The next phase of India's clean-air policy should account for time more explicitly. Government programmes already track expenditure, measures undertaken and changes in pollutant concentrations. They should also ask how quickly an intervention reduces exposure and who is responsible when delivery slips. 

In South Asia, where the economic burden of pollution is already enormous, the value of an intervention depends on where it is deployed, what it tackles and how quickly its benefits reach people. For countries still building their economies, the speed at which cleaner air arrives is itself an economic outcome. 

(The writer is Lead, Subnational and Arctic Program, Gateway Research Institute)

editorials.title: BRICS beyond the rhetoric
editorials.passage:
The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi will be judged by whether its promises survive the return of leaders to their capitals. For India, the summit was an opportunity to shape an increasingly consequential forum at a moment when the global economy is being fragmented by tariffs, sanctions, geopolitical conflict and competing technology standards. For the Global South, it was another test of whether BRICS can become more than a platform for dissatisfaction with the existing international order. 

The scale of the grouping is difficult to ignore. BRICS now comprises 11 countries i.e. Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and UAE, representing about 49.5 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and 26 per cent of global trade, according to Indian government data. Its enlarged membership spans Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. But size alone does not create influence. The central question after Delhi is whether such diversity can become practical cooperation. India’s presidency attempted to move BRICS in that direction. More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were held across 25 Indian cities during the year. The New Delhi Declaration placed resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability at the centre of the agenda, while supporting work on health, food and energy security, artificial intelligence, climate action, industrial cooperation and financial resilience. 

Such an agenda is relevant to developing countries, where shocks often mean higher food bills, expensive energy, disrupted supply chains or reduced access to capital. For India, the immediate gain may be diplomatic. New Delhi has long pursued strategic autonomy, working with the United States, Europe and Japan while retaining substantial relationships with Russia and engaging China despite bilateral tensions. BRICS provides another room in which India can speak simultaneously to several parts of the developing world. The diverse membership widens India's diplomatic reach. 

This matters because many developing economies are seeking greater policy space without severing access to Western markets, capital, technology, institutions, expertise and established supply chains. Yet BRICS also exposes India’s constraints. China remains the grouping’s largest economic power, and the expanded membership includes states whose interests do not always converge with New Delhi’s. Reuters noted after the summit that the Delhi meeting was diplomatically useful for India but also gave China a platform to showcase its influence. That ambiguity is fundamental to BRICS: it gives India a larger voice while also magnifying that of its strategic competitor. The economic agenda may ultimately prove more consequential. 

The summit stopped short of the frequently discussed idea of a common BRICS currency. Instead, members backed greater use of local currencies in trade and investment and continued work on interoperable cross-border payment systems. This is more modest, but potentially more practical. A common currency would require extraordinary monetary and political convergence; cheaper, faster payment mechanisms require far less integration. For India, better cross-border payments could reduce transaction costs and ease trade. India also supported a BRICS Risk Lab at Gujarat's GIFT City. 

The summit encouraged the New Development Bank to expand local-currency financing and diversify funding sources. These steps matter because developing countries face infrastructure -finance gaps and currency mismatches. The New Development Bank could become one of BRICS’s most tangible instruments for the Global South. The bank's role has been reaffirmed as a source of infrastructure and sustainable-development finance, while the BRICS-NDB Knowledge Portal launched during India's chairship is intended to share development experience and policy innovations. 

The opportunity is to create an additional source of patient capital and development knowledge for emerging economies. The technology agenda is equally important. Artificial intelligence is becoming a source of productivity, but computing power, advanced chips and frontier models remain concentrated in a few countries and firms. BRICS's emphasis on inclusive and equitable access to AI, alongside India's push for digital public infrastructure cooperation, could help developing countries avoid becoming merely consumers of imported technologies. India's digital public infrastructure offers a model, though differences in regulation and state capacity will complicate replication. There is also a larger geopolitical significance. 

The declaration called for reform of global institutions and greater representation for developing countries. BRICS countries represented around 27 per cent of world GDP and nearly 45 per cent of global population in 2023, according to India's Commerce Ministry, while exports to BRICS markets accounted for nearly 18 per cent of India's total exports. The grouping therefore matters to India's trade as well as its diplomacy. But expectations should remain calibrated. BRICS is not a conventional alliance, nor does it have the institutional cohesion of the European Union. Its members differ sharply over security interests, economic systems, relations with the West and regional rivalries. 

Consensus language can therefore conceal difficult implementation questions. Announcements on local- currency trade, payment interoperability, AI cooperation or development finance will matter only if ministries, banks, businesses and institutions translate them into operating systems. That is the real test for India after Delhi. Having used its presidency to expand the agenda, New Delhi now has to help build mechanisms that continue beyond its chairmanship. BRICS’s credibility will depend on measurable gains in trade, investment, finance, technology cooperation and resilience, not declarations. For the Global South, the stakes are broader. 

The world needs institutions that can finance infrastructure, reduce payment friction, share technology and strengthen resilience. BRICS cannot replace the multilateral system, but it can make that system less concentrated and more responsive if it produces usable alternatives rather than rhetorical ones. Delhi has therefore given BRICS a larger stage. India’s challenge is to turn that stage into an institutional workshop. The summit’s value will ultimately lie in giving emerging economies more room to finance, trade, innovate and negotiate in a fragmented world. 

The writer is a consultant to Rashtriya Raksha University under the Ministry of Home Affairs, a civil engineer and a contemporary affairs commentator. The views are personal.

editorials.title: Mandate Myth
editorials.passage:
A parliamentary election can strengthen a government’s authority without necessarily demonstrating the breadth of its popular support. Russia’s latest electoral exercise illustrates this distinction, raising questions not merely about the composition of its legislature but about the political consequences of allowing the Kremlin to equate electoral victory with national consent. United Russia’s anticipated retention of its constitutional majority in the State Duma comes amid a prolonged war in Ukraine, mounting economic pressures and attacks on Russian infrastructure. 

These circumstances might ordinarily create political opportunities for opposition parties to question the government’s strategic choices. Yet the absence of meaningful electoral competition has sharply restricted the possibility of converting public discontent into parliamentary influence. The exclusion of Yabloko, the only anti-war party permitted to enter the electoral contest before its removal from the party list, exposes the institutional limitations of Russian political pluralism. Although some of its candidates continued to contest individual constituencies, the party’s marginalisation substantially narrowed the space for an organised challenge to the Kremlin’s war policy. A legislature dominated by parties that support the government cannot adequately represent the full range of public concerns simply by virtue of being elected. 

This distinction matters because the political value of an election extends beyond the allocation of parliamentary seats. Competitive elections provide a mechanism for testing public opinion, holding governments accountable and offering peaceful alternatives to existing policies. When these functions are weakened, electoral victories risk becoming instruments of political validation rather than meaningful tests of consent. For President Vladimir Putin, the parliamentary outcome offers an opportunity to reinforce the appearance of national unity behind the war. 

A compliant Duma can endorse government decisions, approve legislation and provide institutional support for policies whose consequences extend well beyond Russia’s borders. But parliamentary unanimity should not be mistaken for an absence of disagreement within society. The war’s economic costs, military casualties and disruption of civilian life create pressures that electoral arithmetic cannot resolve. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, including facilities around Moscow, also demonstrate that the conflict’s consequences are no longer confined to distant battlefields. 

The possibility of renewed mobilisation remains particularly sensitive, despite Putin’s public assurance that another wave is not presently necessary. The central danger is that the Kremlin may interpret its electoral success as permission to continue the existing course indefinitely. A government insulated from effective political scrutiny has fewer institutional incentives to reconsider costly policies, acknowledge setbacks or accommodate dissent. 

 That does not make escalation inevitable, but it increases the possibility of decisions being taken within a narrow circle of power. Russia’s election has therefore strengthened the formal position of the ruling establishment without settling the fundamental question of how much sacrifice the public will tolerate. The Duma may provide the Kremlin with parliamentary endorsement, but it cannot guarantee enduring social consent. In a prolonged war, that distinction could become increasingly consequential. Electoral control can secure legislative obedience; it cannot, by itself, secure victory in Ukraine, economic stability or lasting domestic legitimacy.

editorials.title: German warning
editorials.passage:
Germany’s fragile economic recovery is unfolding alongside a deepening crisis of political confidence. The latest state elections raise a question extending beyond Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s fortunes: can economic improvement restore faith in established parties when voters remain uncertain about their future? The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44 per cent in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, followed by another breakthrough in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 20, where it secured 38.2 per cent. Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) received just 4.9 per cent there, falling below the threshold for parliamentary representation. 

In Berlin, far Left Die Linke came first with 25.7 per cent, ahead of the CDU’s 18.8 per cent; the AfD finished third with 16.3 per cent. These contrasting results reveal discontent taking different political forms. The CDU’s collapse in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is a major setback for the party leading Germany’s federal government. Merz has called the outcome a disaster but insists that his coalition with the Social Democrats must endure and that reforms must proceed. His determination to remain in office, however, cannot resolve the underlying crisis of confidence. 

The real question is whether Germany’s economic recovery could outrun the AfD. The difficulty is that improvement in national indicators does not necessarily translate into greater security for households. Weak domestic demand, high energy costs, industrial restructuring and uncertainty continue to weigh on businesses and workers. Years of anxiety about employment, public services and future prospects cannot be erased by modest growth. In eastern Germany, demographic decline and the uneven experience of reunification compound economic concerns. The AfD has channelled discontent into a narrative that blames migration, established parties and distant institutions. Economic distress alone cannot explain its rise, but repeated electoral gains suggest that established parties have struggled to convince many voters they understand their concerns. 

Berlin offers a different dimension. Die Linke’s victory, with housing affordability prominent in its campaign, demonstrates that dissatisfaction with established politics does not automatically translate into support for the far right. Housing costs and urban pressures generate their own political demands. Germany’s electoral shifts cannot be reduced to a single national explanation. Merz faces a difficult balance. His government argues that pension, labour-market and public-finance reforms are necessary, alongside infrastructure investment. Yet reforms whose costs are immediate and benefits uncertain can intensify resistance. Abandoning change may perpetuate economic weakness; pursuing it without public confidence may further erode support. 

The AfD’s advance also shows that excluding it from governing coalitions cannot, by itself, address the grievances behind its support. Nor would adopting its positions guarantee solutions. Democratic parties must demonstrate that they can govern competently and respond to legitimate concerns. Germany’s warning is therefore larger than one election or one chancellor. Economic recovery and political confidence are not interchangeable. Growth must become tangible in people’s lives, and reforms must be explained honestly, with their costs acknowledged and benefits made visible. Improving statistics isn’t enough. Citizens must feel that the future offers them security and a meaningful stake.

editorials.title: Inner rumblings
editorials.passage:
For more than a year, I have written critically about the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls: its de novo character, its documentary burdens, its treatment of electors photo identity cards (EPIC), its emphasis on deletion and, finally, the extraordinary numbers left out of electoral rolls.

The disclosures this week raise an even more fundamental question. The issue is no longer only about whether particular decisions of the Election Commission of India were wise, fair or legally sustainable. It is whether decisions taken in the name of the Election Commission were, in fact, decisions by the Election Commission.

“Who was authorised to file these appeals on behalf of ECI, and by whom?”

That question was reportedly recorded on file by the election commissioner, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu, in relation to West Bengal.

The numbers explain why it matters. Of the 27.16 lakh voters deleted during the SIR, 22.21 lakh appealed for restoration. Another 16.10 lakh appeals sought deletion of voters whom the judicial officers had included. The EC’s affidavit did not disclose who filed this second category. Sandhu reportedly asked who had authorised appeals “on behalf of ECI” and who had actually filed them. Neither he or the other election commissioner, Vivek Joshi, nor the present chief electoral officer of West Bengal, Sandhu reportedly recorded, had been informed of the basis or of the process.

This is not an office quarrel. It goes to the legal identity of the EC itself.

The Indian Express has reported that Sandhu and Joshi recorded objections at least 14 times in 10 months to actions they said were taken without their knowledge. These concerned matters at the heart of electoral administration: registration and deletion of voters, Form 6, restoration of names, appeals and control over the digital architecture of the electoral rolls.

The law leaves little ambiguity about how the EC is supposed to function. Section 18 of the 2023 Act provides that its business shall, as far as possible, be transacted unanimously. Where members differ, the decision shall be according to the opinion of the majority. Even the procedure governing transaction and allocation of business requires unanimity.

The chief election commissioner, therefore, chairs a constitutional Commission; he is not a substitute for it.

The Supreme Court put the principle memorably in T.N. Seshan vs Union of India in 1995: “It would be wrong to project the individual and eclipse the Election Commission.”

That distinction becomes crucial here. If one commissioner disagrees with the other two, the majority prevails. But if two commissioners say that they were bypassed, they are not a dissenting minority. They constitute the statutory majority.

Consider Form 6. Joshi reportedly objected that a statutory form prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules could not be altered through an administrative SIR direction without amending the Rules. Sandhu concurred. Yet the altered version appeared on ECINet. Sandhu later described the change as “unauthorised and illegal” and sought its removal.

Or consider technology. Electoral registration officers (EROs) are the statutory authorities empowered to decide additions, deletions and corrections. Yet the two commissioners reportedly raised concerns about database control being centralised in Delhi. In Goa, the names of 97 persons whom EROs had found eligible could reportedly not be restored because the software would not permit the officers to record their decisions.

Technology can facilitate statutory authority. It cannot replace it. A computer portal cannot quietly become superior to the officer whom Parliament has vested with the power to decide.

The Commission’s response to the disclosures makes the institutional question still more important.

Initially, reports citing unnamed ECI “sources” asserted that all SIR decisions had been taken unanimously with the approval of all three commissioners. There was something almost self-defeating about answering a controversy over who could speak for the EC through unidentified persons speaking for the Commission.

Later, on the same day, came a formal press note stating that differences of opinion were part of normal deliberation and that all decisions of the full Commission had been unanimous during the past year.

That is certainly preferable to anonymous briefing. But it does not completely resolve the issue.

The statement was issued in the Commission’s name through an officer. It does not tell us whether Sandhu and Joshi themselves approved this particular response. Ordinarily, that might be an unnecessary question. But it becomes relevant because the reported file records include objections by the two commissioners themselves to communications and actions being undertaken in the Commission’s name without requisite approval.

More importantly, the press note does not reconcile the apparent contradiction. On one side are reported file notings saying that the two commissioners were unaware of particular actions. On the other is the official assertion that all decisions of the full Commission were unanimous.

Both propositions could conceivably coexist if some actions preceded formal decisions, or were taken under a valid allocation of business. But that is precisely why the documentary record matters.

The EC can settle the controversy easily. It should disclose which major SIR decisions were approved by the full Commission; what allocation of business authorised actions were taken without reference to all three members; who authorised the West Bengal appeals; and what actual authority EROs retain over ECINet.

I must also revise one assumption of my own. Watching the Commission maintain a united public face, I had sometimes wondered whether the silence of the two election commissioners meant acquiescence. The reported file records suggest that the conclusion was too easy. Whether they should have spoken publicly earlier is another matter; objections formally recorded on file matter greatly.

The larger issue transcends SIR and the personalities presently occupying the Commission.

We rightly worry about the independence of the EC from the executive. But institutional independence also requires safeguards against unilateralism within the institution itself.

A multi-member EC was created for a reason. Collective authority is not an administrative inconvenience. It is a constitutional safeguard.

The EC asks nearly a billion voters to comply scrupulously with electoral law. It must demonstrate the same scrupulousness in establishing that every consequential act done in its name actually carries the authority of the EC.

S.Y. Quraishi is a former chief election commissioner of India

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Singapore's reading push to fight brain rot, doomscrolling
editorials.passage:
Sir — Singapore has devised a scheme to get people to put down their cellphones and pick up a book. The government is encouraging citizens to read for at least 15 minutes a day to fight brain rot and doomscrolling. A reading of 15 minutes earns 20 virtual coins, with 1000 coins eventually amounting to a Singapore dollar. The sum is hardly a fortune, but the intent is to turn reading into a habit through rewards and gratification. However, when tied to extrinsic reward, reading may not offer the deeper enrichment of the soul that comes from reading for its own sake. What happens when the gravy train stops chugging?

Sir — If the national song, “ Vande Mataram ”, has been accorded the same status as the national anthem, “ Jana Gana Mana ”, then why should we feel ashamed to sing its full version? (“SC: No penalty for Vande denial”, Sept 23). If the last four stanzas of “ Vande Mataram ” are considered problematic because of their references to the imagery of Hindu goddesses, then the entire song should be rejected. The partial rendition of the national song is disrespectful.

Sir — The Supreme Court firmly cited the landmark 1986 Bijoe Emmanuel versus State of Kerala judgment to reiterate that individuals who respectfully decline to sing “ Vande Mataram ” on conscientious grounds should not face criminal prosecution or penalties. The attempt by the Bharatiya Janata Party to alter history and law is shameful. The initial stanzas of “ Vande Mataram ” focus on the abundance of the land while the latter stanzas contain references to Hindu deities that is in conflict with the theological beliefs of monotheistic faiths such as Islam and Christianity.

Further, the use of the term, “Naxalite”, by the solicitor-general of India, Tushar Mehta, to describe the opponent during the court hearing was inappropriate. It echoes the prime minister’s recent coinage of the phrase, “ dimaagi Naxal”. It is unfortunate that Mehta is using the BJP IT cell rhetoric in the Supreme Court.

Bidyut Kumar Chatterjee, Faridabad

Sir — The Supreme Court verdict on “ Vande Mataram ” underscores that the Constitution of India continues to protect individual freedoms even when legislative mandates test the limits of conscience. By ruling that a conscientious objector cannot be penalised for refusing to sing the national song and by sending a notice to the Centre in this regard, the apex court has defended the secular architecture of the republic. This vital intervention proves that judicial review continues to vigorously check parliamentary overreach and preserve absolute liberty of conscience.

Sir — A top court bench headed by the chief justice of India that was hearing T.M. Krishna’s plea challenging the new law mandating the singing of all six stanzas of the national song has upheld constitutional freedom. Forcing citizens of a faith other than Hinduism to sing the last four stanzas of the national song risks imposing a patriotic test that is in contradiction to secularism and religious freedom. Respect for the nation must be voluntary. National symbols should reflect India’s pluralism.

Sir — It is surprising to see a particular party and ideology that had little connection with the freedom struggle or the patriotic songs of that era place such strong emphasis on “ Vande Mataram ” today. The BJP’s insistence on singing the entire song has sparked religious polarisation.

Jang Bahadur Singh, Jamshedpur

Sir — World Alzheimer’s Day is observed on Sept­ember 21. But awareness about the disease is no longer enough. Does our healthcare system offer a clear, connected path from diagnosis to care and support? Early identification is important, but so is the journey that follows. Technology offers possibilities. With informed consent and strong safeguards for personal data, a unique patient identification system could help ensure that essential medical history and treatment details remain accessible. Another urgent concern is the patients who go missing because of memory loss. A coordinated mechanism linking families, health centres, police and local administration could help locate and reunite such patients faster.

A.K. Mookherjee, North 24 Parganas

Sir — Angh , set in Nagaland, is in the race at the 99th Academy Awards following its recognition at the Toronto International Film Festival. It is a great moment for India, particularly for a film emerging from the culturally distinctive landscape of Nagaland. At the heart of Angh is a father-son duo living a secluded life in a village sustained by traditional customs. Their self-contained existence is confronted by the arrival of an American. For Indian cinema, a journey from Nagaland to Toronto and, now, to the Oscars is indeed a remarkable moment.

Vijay Singh Adhikari, Nainital

editorials.title: Skills to hone
editorials.passage:
India’s youth, aged 18-29, make up 27% of its population. They can become India’s ‘demographic dividend’ only if they acquire the skills needed for meaningful employment. Around 28-30% of this cohort has completed higher education. The rest need employable skills through vocational education. Industrial Training Institutes, the backbone of India’s vocational training system, have around 15,000 centres. Of these, 78% are privately operated. Their courses, generally lasting one or two years and aimed mostly at Class VIII-X pass-outs, primarily serve manufacturing.

But the system has failed to keep pace with the talent needs of manufacturing and services because of the disconnect between ITI curricula and industry needs; outdated laboratories and tool rooms; a chronic shortage of instructors and refresher courses; and underutilisation, with many seats lying vacant. To address these demands, the Centre launched the Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM SETU) in October 2025. The Central scheme entails an investment of Rs 60,000 crore to upgrade 1,000 government ITIs through private participation, using a hub-and-spoke model of 200 hubs and 800 spokes. Supported by the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, it aims to equip at least two million young people with contemporary skills over five years.

The scheme seeks to deli­ver demand-driven, industry-aligned training and improve governance. Special purpose vehicles (SPVs) will prepare and implement five-year strategic investment plans covering funding, infrastructure, programmes and trainer capacity. Greater autonomy, outcome-based accountability and industry involvement in course design are envisaged. States must strengthen policies, planning and evaluation, mobilise industry and training providers, ensure adequate staffing and enable ITIs to develop customised courses and partnerships. The Centre must strengthen policy coordination, monitoring and evaluation. Funding for each cluster will be divided among the Centre, state and private partner in a 50:33:17 ratio. Since the private partner will implement the investment plan and manage operations, it will hold 51% of the SPV, with the government holding 49%.

Bengal has 315 ITIs: 166 State-owned and the rest private. PM SETU will cover 51 State-operated ITIs, with 11 hubs and 40 spokes. The state has yet to begin selecting private partners through competitive bidding. Bengal’s manufacturing and services requirements must guide this process. Industries may partner with clusters in existing industrial belts to meet their talent needs. Customised courses and facilities on ITI premises would reduce post-recruitment training costs, while contributions to SPVs could come from CSR funds. Established skill-development organisations, however, may struggle to participate as anchor partners on a revenue-generating model. As not-for-profit companies, SPVs allow neither profit repatriation nor dividends. Such organisations must fund upgrades and operations without returns beyond expenses approved by the board. They could instead form consortiums with industrial companies within the bidding framework.

The state must build safeguards into shareholder agreements, SPV governance and board composition. Strong monitoring and reporting must ensure that promised investments are made; approved courses, curricula and teaching methods are introduced; and training standards and outcomes are achieved. Success will depend on whether funding, institutional autonomy and industry participation translate into training that matches actual jobs rather than merely producing another set of certificates. PM SETU could provide West Bengal with employment-ready youth for its expected industrial and economic rejuvenation.

editorials.title: Hot seat: Editorial on India’s UN ambitions and the need for diplomatic clarity
editorials.passage:
A diverse set of voices has been heard from global representatives covering a wide range of subjects at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly that is currently taking place in New York. Some of these voices have spoken on urgent, unfolding global challenges. Others have advocated institutional reform — for the United Nations Security Council. For instance, the foreign ministers of G4 nations — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — met on the sidelines of the UNGA last week to push for structural change within the UNSC. Their contention is that the UNSC, an exclusive club of five veto-empowered nations, is anachronistic under the present circumstances because it has not been able to respond adequately to or resolve the conflicts and the crises that are lacerating the world order and economy. The UNSC’s permanent and non-permanent categories, the G4 countries have demanded, need to be expanded for them to be truly representative. The Indian prime minister had expressed similar sentiments, urging for the reformation of the UNSC at the recent BRICS Summit in New Delhi.

The demand for a more democratic and, consequently, consultative UNSC is not anomalous in a world that is witnessing the ascendancy of multilateral blocs. But a looming contradiction must be noted. New Delhi, undoubtedly, wants a seat at the UN high table. The legitimacy of that demand cannot be dismissed. But such a hot seat would require India to take unambiguous positions on crucial, but also complex, global issues. Such conviction and clarity have been missing from some of New Delhi’s recent utterances. For instance, at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India desisted from calling a spade a spade when it came to the fires in West Asia and Ukraine. This, according to New Delhi’s diplomatic math, is consistent with the equation of strategic autonomy that has much purchase these days. India believes that fence-sitting helps it nurse its ties with a number of nations that are embroiled in mutual antipathies. But this kind of indecisiveness cannot be a shield if New Delhi is to occupy, some day, a chair on a platform of global importance. This is not to suggest that India must shy away from demanding a position of consequence in the UN. But it cannot waver or be evasive once it achieves that goal. Resoluteness has been a traditional strength of Indian diplomacy. It must rediscover that gift.

editorials.title: No penalty: Editorial on Vande Mataram and the limits of compulsion
editorials.passage:
“Conscientious objectors” cannot be penalised. Sitting on a petition challenging the 2026 amendment to Section 3 of the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, which states the penalties for disrupting the singing of “ Vande Mataram ”, the national song, the Supreme Court said that those who refused to sing it because it went against their conscience could not be punished. The penalty according to the new law regarding the song is imprisonment for three years or a fine or both. The Bharatiya Janata Party-led government has made singing all six stanzas of the song mandatory at official and ceremonial functions. The petition from T.M. Krishna, the well-known singer and writer, said that the last four stanzas of the song undermined the secular nature of the nation. The first two stanzas of the song had been accepted as the national song in 1937 by the Indian National Congress; the latter four are invocations to Hindu deities. Hence the government’s insistence that this song be sung in full at all government events has been considered problematic by many. The Supreme Court made it clear that it would not rule on the decision to declare “ Vande Mataram ” as the national song, but only on the imposition of the penalty. The court referred to a 1987 judgment that protected three children who had been expelled from school because they had refused to sing the national anthem; it went against their religion. At that time the Supreme Court had ruled on the basis of freedom of religion and freedom of expression, which included the right to remain silent. The court said that it expected the new law to be governed by the 1987 judgment.

The penal consequences attendant on offences regarding the singing of all six stanzas of “ Vande Mataram ” undermine the principle of equality, as the last four stanzas focus on the majority religion. The Supreme Court’s ruling, by dismissing the penalty, asserts the constitutional right to freedom of conscience and of religion while upholding the right to personal liberty. Although the ruling is on one specific issue, its spirit underlines the importance of conscientious individual choice without the fear of penalties, the rights of minorities and, by implication, the inclusion of difference. At a time when laws often appear to be weaponised, such a ruling infuses trust in constitutional freedoms.

editorials.title: The next phase of Make in India
editorials.passage:
On September 25, 2014, India set a clear ambition: to make for India and make for the world. Twelve years later, Make in India has evolved from an initiative into a national manufacturing mission.

As CII marks this milestone, we see its impact not just in policy documents, but in factories and shopfloors, ports, roads and highways and in new jobs created across the country.

The vision of Make in India is backed by consistent and coordinated action on four pillars:

The first is ease of doing business. More than 47,000 compliances have been reduced as of November 2025, including 16,108 simplified, 22,287 digitised, 4,458 decriminalised and 4,270 redundant compliances removed. The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2026 further strengthens trust-based governance by decriminalising 717 provisions and amending 784 provisions across 79 Central Acts.

Further, the National Single Window System now integrates approvals across 32 Central Ministries and 34 States/UTs, covering over 686 Central and 7,498 State approvals. Complementing this, the Business Reform Action Plan, launched in 2015, has driven States and UTs to simplify regulations and improve transparency across areas including clearances, land, labour, inspections, taxation and environmental approvals.

The second is world-class infrastructure. Dedicated freight corridors, 11 industrial corridors, Sagarmala and Bharatmala projects, and significant expansion of port and airport capacity have brought raw material closer to factories and factories closer to markets. PM Gati Shakti has added coherence to logistics planning and reduced the logistics cost, making manufacturing in India competitive.

The third pillar is digital and tax reforms. GST created one national market, while ONDC and the Unified Logistics Interface Platform created one digital backbone. This has been uniquely an Indian model — physical manufacturing powered by digital public infrastructure.

The fourth pillar is openness to investment. FDI limits were liberalised across defence, railways, insurance, construction and space, boosting access to global capital, technology and expertise. FDI inflows rose to ₹49.46 lakh crore during 2014-24, nearly double the ₹25.40 lakh crore in the previous decade.

A key enabler in this journey has been the Production Linked Incentive scheme. As of June 2026, the scheme has attracted ₹2.58 lakh crore in actual investment, ₹23.79 lakh crore in production and sales, and ₹15.53 lakh crore in exports, while supporting over 14.57 lakh direct and indirect jobs.

In electronics and semiconductors, production of electronic goods has reached ₹13.11 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, with exports of ₹4.24 lakh crore. Simultaneously, the India Semiconductor Mission, with the recently announced outlay of ₹1.27 lakh crore, is building the base that will deepen this value chain further upstream.

In automotive, the Auto PLI scheme has drawn ₹45,477 crore in investment, creating over 67,000 jobs. It promotes high-value advanced automotive technology vehicles and products. India is today the world’s largest producer of two-wheelers and three-wheelers.

In industrial corridor development, introduced in July 2026, the BHAVYA Scheme has an outlay of ₹33,660 crore for five years from FY 2026-27 to 2030-31. It will support the establishment of 100 world-class industrial parks across the country with common essential infrastructure, helping MSMEs scale sustainably.

Support for MSMEs and startups has also remained central to the manufacturing journey. ECLGS 5.0 targets additional credit flow of ₹2.55 lakh crore in response to the West Asia situation. Together with GeM, this has helped in the procurement of over ₹20 lakh crore worth of goods and services through the portal, by catalysing more than three crore orders.

Equally significant has been the growth of India’s innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem. Startup India has enabled over 2.5 lakh recognised startups, generating more than 25 lakh jobs, with nearly half emerging from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities. Digital recognition, a higher ₹200 crore turnover ceiling, a dedicated Deep Tech category and abolition of angel tax have further reduced barriers and strengthened the startup ecosystem.

Research, Development and Innovation is another important building block. The ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund is creating a major platform for private-sector-led R&D, deep-tech and high-impact innovation. This can help India move beyond scale and assembly towards technology-led manufacturing, stronger IP creation and higher domestic value addition.

The signing of nine FTAs in six years spanning 38 countries has added further momentum by expanding preferential market access for Indian manufacturers and exporters across sectors. These agreements can help Indian manufacturing integrate more deeply into global value chains, diversify export destinations, and scale up production for international markets, thereby creating new opportunities for Indian industry and supporting India’s ambition of achieving $1 trillion in merchandise exports. To make this success sustainable, the focus must now be on effective implementation and greater utilisation of these agreements by industry.

CII has been advocating a focused agenda to Government for the next phase of Make in India. These would include:

First, enhancing domestic manufacturing depth. While final assembly has scaled, we must deepen value addition in components, raw materials, precision parts and capital goods, with stronger linkages between large OEMs and MSME suppliers.

Second, cluster-based approach for exports. India needs world-class manufacturing clusters with plug-and-play infrastructure, testing labs, logistics and worker housing, focused on export markets. Clusters in electronics, textiles, auto components, chemicals and engineering can help reduce logistics cost and build scale for FTAs.

Third, trust-based economic governance. Non-Financial Regulatory Reforms (NFRR) and the Jan Vishwas Act cohesively build strategy for administrative simplification coupled with legislative decriminalization. This should continue.

Fourth, AI and automation for smart manufacturing. The next leap in competitiveness will come from adoption of AI, automation and Industry 4.0. CII is advocating for support to MSMEs to adopt smart manufacturing tools, predictive maintenance, digital twins and AI-led quality control. Linking the AI Mission with manufacturing, creating shared Industry 4.0 facilities in clusters, and skilling workers for human-machine collaboration will help India move from cost competitiveness to technology competitiveness.

Twelve years ago, we began with an idea. Today, we have a thriving ecosystem. With new building blocks and focus on domestic depth, export clusters, financial reforms and smart manufacturing, we are strengthening the foundation for the next decade.

Make in India has given India the confidence that we can make, we can make well, and we can make for the world. This is no mean achievement.

The writer is Director General, Confederation of Indian Industry

Published on September 25, 2026

editorials.title: India’s forest plans need a better architect
editorials.passage:
India has become good at counting forests but the numbers conceal an important distinction. There is a difference between having more forest area and having more forest cover. FAO’s Global Forest Resources Assessment (GFRA) 2025, for instance, stated that India ranks ninth globally in terms of Total Forest Area and third globally in Annual Net Gain of Forest Area. A gain in forest area does not necessarily mean a gain in forest cover and the same need not translate into a healthier forest ecosystem.

The Indian picture, however, looks remarkably different when the lens shifts to the other side of the spectrum. The recent CAG performance audit of the Green India Mission tabled in the Parliament on August 12 revealed that against a target of 1.4 million hectares, improvement in quality of forest cover was observed in only 0.11 mha. The increase in forest cover itself was even smaller, only 0.03 mha against the target of 1.4 mha. This stark contrast raises concerns beyond India’s actual numbers.

The Green India Mission (GIM) is more than just a tree planting programme. It is one of the primary agendas of the NAPCC (National Action Plan for Climate Change) through which India seeks to increase forest and tree cover and ultimately enhance carbon sequestration and biodiversity. The 98 per cent shortfall is striking. However, this has also raised a more fundamental concern, as for ecological restoration, where a tree is planted is almost as important as whether a tree is planted. Even when trees were planted under GIM, 70 per cent of the sampled sites showed no improvement.

This is despite the existence of a dedicated GIS cell for monitoring the scheme. What is more troubling is that this is a pattern that is evident across India where a plantation is often being confused with restoration.

The plantation versus restoration matters particularly for India’s climate commitments. The country committed to create an additional carbon sink of 3.5-4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through additional forest and tree cover by 2035. However, a hectare of trees planted does not automatically convert to a tonne of carbon sequestrated. Carbon storage relies deeply on what existed on the land before, the species selected, their survival, soil conditions, water availability and maturity of the ecosystem. The planting of trees on a piece of land is not the same as creating an equivalent carbon sink to the atmosphere.

India’s forest governance vastly depends on a similar implicit bargain, when a forest land is diverted for development, compensatory afforestation is taken elsewhere. The Great Nicobar Project seeks to transform the island into a strategic maritime and economic hub at the cost of diverting 1.82 per cent of pristine tropical rainforests. Since the island already has 75 per cent forest cover, the compensatory afforestation is planned kilometres away in an entirely different mainland, Haryana.

The logic may sound straightforward but ecological restoration does not work like balancing two columns in accounts. These incidents are also not isolated events. In Maharashtra, the State approved diversion of nearly 83,700 sq ft of forest land including reserve forests and mangrove land for a proposed cement terminal in Alibag. Similarly, large-scale felling of the protected Satbari area of the Delhi ridge in the capital for urban and infrastructure expansion led to penalty of 1.67 lakh trees. The missing element here is that the newly planted cannot immediately replicate the microclimate, soil composition or biodiversity of a mature natural green space. It merely satisfies an administrative requirement. Even when interventions were made under GIM, afforestation target of only 0.28 mha was achieved against the objective of 2.8 mha which was to be completed by 2018.

Another overlooked concern here is the consequences for biodiversity, particularly wildlife. It matters for wildlife that there is a continuous, useable habitat. The fragmentation of forest corridors has time and again shown that even when tree cover exists, interruptions in habitat reduce wildlife movement. Wildlife species depend on native vegetation, canopy structure, undergrowth, water availability and ecological connectivity that newly created monocultures will not be able to provide. An elephant or a tiger would not recognise a man-made boundary. It often appears as human-wildlife conflict, it is however more of a connectivity and unplanned restoration shortcoming.

This is the core weakness of treating forest cover or any ecological conservation more broadly, as a numerical target. For climate, biodiversity and restoration, geography is always part of the equation. India should also make far greater use of existing satellites and geospatial capabilities it already possesses. If compensatory afforestation becomes the primary mechanism for producing more hectares on paper, it risks weakening rather than strengthening the environmental bargain underlying the forest diversion. Climate-vulnerability and biodiversity maps need to become part of the approval process.

The solution is not simply to provide a single mission with more money even though funding clearly matters. The mission received only around ₹1,149 crore in the 10 years of implementation counter to the estimated requirement of ₹10,600 crore. However, more money flowing through the same structural gaps would only mean more hectares without any substantial benefits. Survival rates, biomass growth, native-species recovery, soil and water conservations matter more than the number of saplings distributed.

The important lesson here is that any kind of ecological restoration cannot be managed like a construction target. It needs to move away from the idea of simply planting more trees. It needs to harness the skills of where a tree can deliver the greatest ecological value. The real audit is not how many trees it plants but how many functioning ecosystems it preserves.

Kapoor is chair, and Gauratra is researcher, Institute for Competitiveness

Published on September 25, 2026

editorials.title: How AI is redrawing the IT services map
editorials.passage:
The pyramid model is gone. With coding agents, we no longer need basic coding — this blunt assessment comes from V Balakrishnan, the former CFO of Infosys. It is more than a prediction about entry-level jobs. For three decades, Indian IT services built scale by selling engineering capacity, measured largely through hours, utilisation and headcount. If AI can deliver the same work with fewer people, the industry isn’t simply becoming more productive. The economics of what it sells are changing.

That change is already challenging the foundation of the model. Indian IT’s advantage was never just cheap labour; it also rested on scarce skills. AI now attacks both, cutting the hours many tasks require and reducing the scarcity of the skills behind them. Work that once required a specialist can increasingly be handled by a much larger pool of AI augmented generalists. When a scarce input becomes abundant, pricing power comes under pressure.

Nasscom President Rajesh Nambiar is right that AI may redraw India’s IT services map. But the claim that 20 to 25 per cent of firms could struggle to cross over risks making a structural disruption look more bounded than it is. The harder question is how much of the existing model can survive while its replacement is being built.

AI also reduces the opacity around effort, letting clients ask why they’re paying for 10 days of work that now takes two. Under hourly billing, that efficiency gain flows to the client as a lower price, not to the vendor as margin. Pricing towards value delivered is the obvious response, but it shifts delivery risk onto the vendor and demands capabilities the old model never built.

AI creates three pressures at once: fewer hours, less scarcity in the skills behind them and a growing client ability to insource what they once bought. The third is the most disruptive since it threatens intermediation itself, not just delivery cost.

Pricing alone cannot fix this: shifting from hours to outcomes only captures value from work that still exists; it doesn’t guarantee that work, its pricing power, or the relationship will survive insourcing. Building an outcome-based business demands proprietary IP, domain expertise, customer intimacy and delivery risks the old model never had to carry. “Sell outcomes, not people” is an attractive answer. It is not a complete one.

The old revenue model can weaken before the new one becomes viable: legacy revenue disappears quickly, while proprietary platforms and outcome contracts take years to build. A firm can do everything right and still fail if old revenue disappears faster than its replacement emerges.

Much of what passes for transformation today is automation, not redesign. A copilot writes code, an agent triages tickets and the process gets cheaper, but the organisation and pricing model underneath stay untouched. Redesign changes who owns the outcome and the risk, cannibalising the revenue that built the company’s success. Firms can automate without redesigning, then present one as evidence of the other. Automation buys time. It does not guarantee a future.

Underneath sits a structural problem: the classic pyramid (many juniors, fewer seniors, thin leadership) was built to staff hours, not organise accountability for outcomes.

The five largest Indian IT firms added a net 12,718 employees in FY25; in FY26 they shed 6,981. AI is driving that reversal by attacking routine work at the base, while an outcome-oriented organisation needs a smaller, senior-heavy, domain-aware shape that takes years to build.

The people inside that flattening pyramid hear a reassuring half truth: AI won’t replace you if you learn to use it. Clients that once bought hours from Indian vendors are increasingly building their own Global Capability Centres and hiring talent directly since AI lets smaller teams deliver more. “Jobs are just moving up the value chain” is inadequate: AI fluency protects the skill, not the job, when the business model itself is losing relevance.

Much of this stays underexamined because almost nobody is incentivised to say it plainly. A CEO has little reason to tell an earnings call that the core business is shrinking; analysts and consultants have reason to keep the story optimistic. That may explain the appeal of the 20 to 25 per cent estimate, too: it gives a complex transition a reassuring boundary. The more useful question isn’t what percentage fails, but how much value disappears before replacement value emerges, and who captures it.

The real risk is dislocation: can the economy absorb displaced labour and capital as quickly as the old model releases them? A demand recovery won’t restore the old headcount-to-revenue link, and a client with its own GCC has little reason to rebuild it. The long-term outcome may be positive. The transition can still be brutal.

The harder questions are economic: how much revenue exists only because human effort is sold by the hour, what happens as clients insource that effort and whether replacement revenue can scale fast enough to matter. Indian IT can transform, and some firms will build businesses more valuable than what came before. But that doesn’t mean the industry will cross the bridge intact. The real question is how much of it survives long enough to make the transition. AI may redraw India’s IT services map. The damage will not be evenly shared.

The writer is GM and Head AI Lab – Hitachi India. Views are personal
