editorials.title: Why didn’t the Supreme Court stop the SIR?
editorials.passage:
Welcome to The India Fix by Shoaib Daniyal, a newsletter on Indian politics. As always, if you’ve been sent this newsletter and like it, to get it in your inbox every week, sign up here (click on “follow”).

Have feedback, interesting links or think I am wrong? Write to me: theindiafix@scroll.in

On Wednesday, the Indian Express published a bombshell investigation showing that two election commissioners were in revolt against the Special Intensive Revision of the voters rolls being spearheaded by the chief of the panel.

The SIR is an unprecedented reworking of India’s electoral rolls. Under the exercise, crores of Indians have been denied the right to vote. The Indian Express investigation, more than anything else, revealed one dynamic: the Special Intensive Revision was centralising the preparation of the voter rolls. The two commissioners themselves pointed out that this was illegal. Indian law is clear that rolls are created locally by an electoral registration officer.

This problem was brought to the notice of the courts several times. It is a basic function of the judiciary to review administrative acts to ensure that they are in line with existing laws. In this case, the law was in black and white – and it was clear that it was being ignored.

Why did the courts decline to act?

The controversy started in 2025 when in both Bihar and West Bengal , journalistic reports made it clear that electoral registration officers were not the ones deciding which names would be included or deleted names during the SIR. In one case, local officials in Bengal even wrote to the Election Commission pointing out that the deletions were “system-driven”, referring to the panel’s software, rather than being carried out by the electoral registration officer.

The Bengal SIR was intensely litigated in the Supreme Court. What happened when this blatant illegality was brought to the bench’s notice? As my colleague Anant Gupta pointed out , the court simply accepted at “face value” the Election Commission’s assertion that there was no illegality. And that was that.

Incredibly, when a similar challenge was brought to the court with respect to the Bihar SIR, the court actually said it was acceptable for the Election Commission not to follow the law since in the new process the “substance [of the law] remains intact”. It never explained how limiting the powers of electoral registration officers maintained the “substance” of a procedure that is designed to be local.

The local versus central pivot is an obvious candidate for judicial review, given how clearly the SIR is contravening Indian law. But this is only the tip of the iceberg. As legal scholar Gaurav Mukherjee points out , there were several points at which the courts should have stopped the SIR.

The Election Commission had no legal justification for creating arbitrary exclusion norms such as so-called logical discrepancies. Logical discrepancies refer to elements in the records that the panel considers inconsistencies, such as a mismatch with the spellings of names of the voters’ parents, an unreasonably low gap between the ages of parents and children or if parents have more than six children.

Even more egregious is the overwhelming empirical evidence that this process targeted Muslims in Bengal, violating the Supreme Court ruling that there should be “no identity-based exclusion from the rolls and the right to vote of adult citizens”.

Remarkably, during the Bengal SIR hearings, a Supreme Court judge remarked that even if the right to vote was taken away in this election, people wrongfully excluded could come back and vote in the future. As if in a democracy, the right to vote can be arbitrarily denied and then reinstated on a whim.

The effect of the Supreme Court’s abdication of judicial review has been disastrous.

In Bengal, since the process singled out Muslims, the SIR was a significant shot in the arm for the Bharatiya Janata Party since the community does not, as past data shows, large vote for the Hindutva party. It went on to register a shock victory in a state it had never won before.

In a regression analysis of the Bengal SIR published by Scroll in June, academics Bhanu Joshi and Neelanjan Sircar showed that there was a “strong relationship” between the SIR deletions and results: “constituencies where the electoral roll shrank more also saw the BJP do better relative to its main challenger, the Trinamool Congress”.

This arbitrary and illegal exercise has taken away the right to vote for lakhs of Indians. Given the pace of appeals, it might take years, even decades, for them to get it back. Of the appeals decided till now, an overwhelming number – 91% – have seen deletions being reversed , an indication of the scale of just how erroneous the SIR was.

While the conduct of the Supreme Court in allowing an illegal act like the SIR might be unfortunate, it is not surprising.

India’s judiciary makes a lot of noise about being the most powerful in the world and often tom-toms its role as a defender of rights. Yet, in practice, for many decades now, we have seen strong empirical evidence that in actual conduct, the higher judiciary is an organ that, more often than not, meekly follows the executive .

This is especially true if there is a strong government in place. This was evident in 1976, when the Supreme Court fell over itself to rubberstamp Indira Gandhi’s Emergency and its excesses. It was left to politicians and activists to oppose the suppression of rights, and eventually it was voters who kicked Gandhi out of office.

Of course, with an even more authoritarian government in place today, the court is reinforcing its history of timidity. In the Narendra Modi era, judges have made sure never to step on the toes of the executive.

If the situation is to change, as it did in 1977 when Gandhi called off the Emergency, the change will have to come from a place other than the court on New Delhi’s Tilak Road.

editorials.title: Tishani Doshi’s poetry collection ‘Egrets, While War’ is shortlisted for the 2026 PEN Heaney Prize
editorials.passage:
Indian poet Tishani Doshi’s latest book, Egrets, While War , is shortlisted for the 2026 PEN Heaney Prize.

The prize, instituted in 2024, recognises a single volume of poetry by one author, published in the UK or Ireland, of outstanding literary merit that engages with the impact of cultural or political events on human conditions or relationships. It is open to both original English language collections and those translated into English.

This year’s jury comprises poets Victoria Adukwei Bulley, Vona Groarke and Stephen Sexton.

“Tishani Doshi’s dextrous, vibrant and vital poems delight and shimmer. Across Egrets, While War , the range of her subjects is vast: the ancient and modern co-mingle with poems of personal and civic responsibility,” said the jury. “Throughout, an aviary of sonnets addresses the birds of mythology and literature with grace and invention. Wars, historical and contemporary, provide the contexts for these powerful poems of resistance and humanity.”

The winner will be announced on December 1.

The books on the shortlist are:

Pain Songs by Daniel Sluman (Nine Arches Press)

Dwelling by Máighréad Medbh (Macha Press)

Mer de Glace by Małgorzata Lebda, translated by Mira Rosenthal (Fitzcarraldo Editions)

plastic by Matthew Rice (Fitzcarraldo Editions)

October by Nur Turkmani (Hajar Press)

Egrets, While War by Tishani Doshi (Bloodaxe Press)

editorials.title: Inside America’s accommodation of China
editorials.passage:
Watch closely. You may not see one of these again in your lifetime. When was the last time a top Western power visibly accommodated an Asian power at the top of the table as America is now making space for China?

Japan in the 1980s came close, but not quite. Its growth stuttered in the late 1980s and, by the turn of the 1990s, the ‘lost decade’ began. Thus, the viral photo of President Donald Trump, be-gloved and bending, before an upright President Xi Jinping during the latter’s visit to America (September 23-25), is not merely a misleading photograph, of the kind that some journalists love to play up. It is, in fact, the sign of our times.

Consider what Japan faced when it came close. Washington did not make room; it made demands. The Plaza Accord of 1985 forced the yen upward, trade negotiators hammered Tokyo on semiconductors and cars, and a security-dependent country could not refuse. Japan’s challenge ended because Japan was an ally living under an American umbrella. China is no such thing. It cannot be managed by a currency accord or a phone call from the Treasury. And so, for the first time since it inherited the mantle of Western leadership in 1945, America is doing something it has never done for a non-Western power: negotiating a sharing of the summit.

What is remarkable is not that Trump is doing this. It is that almost nobody in Washington with real power is seriously arguing for the alternative. They won’t because there is now a bipartisan consensus about China’s accommodation in America, even if not everyone spells it out quite in the same way. Additionally, as Pew Research has shown, more Americans feel positively about China than ever.

The idea of a G2 is not new. It was floated in American policy circles around 2008-09, when the financial crisis made Beijing’s balance sheet look like the world’s lifeboat. At the time, it was a fringe notion, and the Obama administration soon pivoted to Asia instead. What has changed is that the G2 has quietly acquired a bipartisan constituency, for four reasons.

First, exhaustion. Both parties now speak to a domestic electorate that has lost faith in open-ended global commitments. The Republican right wants tariffs, borders and the Western Hemisphere; the Democratic left wants industrial policy, jobs and climate spending at home. Neither has an appetite for a generational Cold War with an economy of China’s size.

Second, interdependence that cannot be unwound. The tariff wars of 2025 proved a painful point: when Beijing tightened exports of rare earths and magnets, American manufacturers felt it within weeks. Decoupling became ‘de-risking’, and de-risking is increasingly becoming negotiation. You do not declare total war on your supplier of critical inputs.

Third, the logic of the deal. The Trump instinct is transactional — he himself used the phrase ‘G2’ ahead of his meeting with Xi in Busan last year. The Democratic instinct, from the Biden years, was ‘managed competition’ with ‘guardrails’. Stripped of rhetoric, both describe the same thing: two great powers agreeing on the rules of their rivalry and carving out zones of cooperation on trade, fentanyl, climate and nuclear risk.

Fourth, and most important, the quiet acceptance of limits. America’s defence industrial base cannot currently outproduce China’s shipyards. The fighting in Ukraine and West Asia exposed how thin munitions stockpiles are. A power that recognises the limits of its reach seeks a partner to share the burden of order. Washington is looking at Beijing.

Additionally, and simply put, America’s economic elites are more often than not too deeply entrenched in, or with, China to truly wish to disturb their future earnings.

Here lies the asymmetry. America wants a co-chairman. China does not want to be co-anything.

When the G2 idea was first floated, Beijing politely rejected it. That was not modesty; it was strategy. A G2 implies that China accepts a world whose architecture — the dollar, the Bretton Woods institutions, the alliance systems — was built by America and still largely serves it. To be a co-manager of someone else’s house is not the Chinese ambition.

Look at what Xi has actually built. The Belt and Road Initiative, followed by the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and, most recently, the Global Governance Initiative unveiled at the SCO summit in Tianjin. These are not supplements to the American order. They are the scaffolding of an alternative one. Xi’s oft-repeated view that ‘the East is rising and the West is declining’ is not a slogan; it is a reading of history. And in the older Chinese political imagination, there cannot be two suns in one sky.

So, Beijing will accept the photograph of an American president bending but not quite accept the framing of equals. Every concession Washington makes in pursuit of a G2 is banked in Beijing as evidence of a G1 in formation.

Where does this leave India? The conventional anxiety is that a US-China condominium would marginalise New Delhi, and that India must choose which side to lean on before the music stops. Both fears misread India’s position.

India cannot choose, because its interests are too deeply woven into both. America is India’s largest export market, the destination for its software and services, the home of its most influential diaspora, and a partner in defence, technology and the Quad. Yet China remains among India’s largest trading partners, with a trade deficit running to roughly a hundred billion dollars; Indian pharmaceuticals, electronics, solar and automobiles depend heavily on Chinese inputs. The tariff blows India absorbed from Washington last year and the cautious thaw with Beijing that followed show that neither relationship can be treated as settled, and neither can be abandoned.

But this entanglement is not a weakness. It is the source of India’s leverage.

In a G2 world, the most valuable actor is the one both giants need and neither owns. America needs India as the only democratic economy of scale that can absorb supply chains leaving China. China needs India not to become a fully committed American ally on its southern flank, and needs its market. Every American concession to Beijing raises India’s value to Washington as a hedge; every Chinese push for primacy raises India’s value to the rest of Asia as a counterweight that is not an American proxy.

The task, then, is not to choose but to price. India should extract technology transfer and market access from Washington precisely because it is not locked in. It should extract border stability and investment terms from Beijing precisely because it could lock in. And it should lead the vast middle — the Gulf, Asean, Africa, much of Latin America — which fears both a G2 that ignores it and a G1 that dominates it.

The photograph of the bending president might be remembered as the moment America blinked. India’s opportunity is to be the one power that does not need to bend at all. That’s why I argue that, instead of a mere G2 world, it will soon be a G2.5 world, with India, as of now, being the 0.5.

(Hindol Sengupta is Professor of International Relations at O. P. Jindal Global University. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Head-on | India’s economic story is bigger than its critics admit
editorials.passage:
Anyone reading Indian newspaper op-eds would agree with former RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan that India’s economy is in crisis.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, who takes Rajan seriously, calls India’s economy “dead”. Op-ed writers advise with touching concern that Prime Minister Narendra Modi, at 76, is showing his age and must step aside. They fail to notice that Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge is a sprightly 84.

Online sites and YouTube “influencers” with millions of followers target Modi 24/7 with abuse, mocking memes and AI-generated videos. They then complain that India lacks freedom of speech.

“Godi media” is accused of Modi sycophancy – and in this case, the critics are right. On his 76th birthday on September 17, the call to light divas on every street was cringeworthy.

But lambasting the prime minister – which is perfectly normal in a diverse argumentative democracy like India, Britain or the United States – is different from lambasting India with doctored facts.

India obviously has infirmities: corruption, inflation, unemployment, broken civic governance, over-regulation, and poor law enforcement. These are the collateral debris of a country climbing out of mind-numbing poverty.

But is the Indian economy “dead” as Rahul Gandhi says? Are Indian geopolitical op-ed analysts who conclude that India will always remain a Third World middle power and should hitch its wagon to the West’s AI-powered engine correct in their gloomy, subservient assessment?

These questions are best answered by empirical examination. How is the Indian economy really doing in relation to the rest of the world?

It shows that India is now the world’s second-largest producer of cement and crude steel, and the largest manufacturer of two-wheelers. How about passenger cars? India has sped past Japan and Germany to become the world’s third-largest manufacturer of cars, behind only China and the US.

Let us examine other evidence of a dead economy. Is India a global leader in key domains? It turns out India is the world’s largest vaccine producer by volume, the world’s largest producer of milk, the world’s largest IT services provider, and the world’s second-largest producer of sugar, cotton and food grains.

There is more evidence lurking about for economists like Arvind Subramanian, India’s former chief economic adviser (CEA) and perennial pessimist, to examine. He doesn’t.

India is now the world’s third largest producer of pharmaceuticals and the second largest manufacturer of mobile phones and electronics. So why are economists and geopolitical theorists so gloomy about India’s future prospects?

Some have personal reasons: rejection from former bureaucratic bosses. Others are fuelled by politics or ideology. Analysts who live and work abroad ingratiate themselves with their Western paymasters by looking at India with jaundiced eyes.

In a world wracked by two wars, trade disputes and high oil prices, India’s economy has held up remarkably well. Once war clouds clear, trade stabilises and crude oil prices drop back to $70, India’s economy will obviously get new tailwinds.

Foreign analysts, unencumbered by the deep complexes that blur Indian analysts’ vision, have already spotted this. Last week, Moody’s raised India’s 2027 GDP growth forecast from 6 per cent to 7 per cent. Fitch and S&P followed suit.

Vince Cable, Britain’s former secretary of state for business and trade, wrote this in an op-ed in Hindustan Times on September 23, 2026: “I would argue, based on plausible assumptions, India’s development may well lead to rough parity with China by mid-century in terms of economic size.”

Despite the threat of 100 per cent tariffs from the US, Indian exports are doing better than ever. By weaponising tariffs against India, the US has forced New Delhi to look elsewhere. FTAs with the UK, EU, UAE, Australia, New Zealand, Chile, the GCC and several others have been signed or are awaiting operationalisation.

When the bounce returns to India-US trade, which it inevitably will, India’s trade basket would be full. Already, despite wars and oil, India’s annual exports are nearing $1 trillion. Total merchandise and services exports in the five months between April and August 2026, according to published sources, were $400 billion.

If full-year exports cross $1 trillion, it will be the first time this milestone has been achieved despite a geopolitically and economically turbulent environment.

Why then, stock market traders ask, are foreign investors pulling money out of Indian shares? Why, they ask, is the rupee so weak against the US dollar despite the influx of over $160 billion in the RBI’s recent NRI deposit and swap scheme?

The Indian stock market has given an average annual return over the past 20 years of 750 per cent, a figure that will surprise younger traders. Most may not know that the BSE Sensex crossed 10,000 for the first time on February 6, 2006. It is today at 74,000, a rise of 7.4x despite a fall from 85,000 a year ago.

The compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of the Sensex is 11.2 per cent. Traders say gold has given higher 20-year returns – and they are right. Gold is a store of value and rises when there is a global crisis.

Since Covid in 2020, there hasn’t been a year without a global crisis. Gold has risen from Rs 64,000 in 2020 to Rs 1,51,000 today, lifting its 20-year CAGR.

The government has made the situation worse by imposing an irrelevant STT on stock trading. It has allowed its financial bureaucracy to run amok with stringent rules that slow progress. India has too many laws and too little enforcement. That is why India moves two steps forward and one step backward.

Despite this self-imposed inertia, India will probably be the largest or second-largest manufacturer in almost every key industry by 2030. That will give India’s geopolitical analysts and economists more to complain about.

(The writer is an editor, author and publisher. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The State Cannot Take Away Liberty and Explain It Later: What SC’s Ruling Says
editorials.passage: At the heart of the Supreme Court's judgment in Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v State of Punjab is a simple constitutional proposition: when the State takes away a person's liberty, it must tell him why. In its judgment, the Court has reiterated a long-standing principle of criminal law and constitutional governance that an arrest cannot be divorced from the right of the arrested person to know the basis on which his liberty has been curtailed. Where the State fails to provide that basic information, it cannot then ask the law to treat the resulting detention as though nothing constitutionally significant has occurred.The language of Article 22(1) leaves little room for ambiguity. It requires that a person who is arrested be informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds of arrest and guarantees them the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of their choice. A person who does not know why he has been arrested cannot properly instruct a lawyer, challenge the basis of his custody, oppose a request for police remand or seek appropriate relief from a court.The Supreme Court has, therefore, correctly treated the communication of the grounds of arrest as part of the constitutional architecture protecting personal liberty under Article 21.The Supreme Court's Deliberate Balancing Act on the Protest CrackdownIn Mihir Rajesh Shah, which the Court reaffirmed in the present judgment, the Court made the position clear: the grounds of arrest must ordinarily be furnished in writing, in a language understood by the arrested person, and the obligation is not dependent upon the particular statute under which the arrest is made. The protection travels with the person whose liberty is being curtailed. This matters because an arrest is not simply the beginning of a criminal case. It is the point at which the coercive power of the State is brought physically and immediately to bear upon an individual. Once arrested, a person may be taken into police custody, interrogated, deprived of his ordinary freedom of movement and placed in a position of profound dependence upon the legal system for his release. It is precisely at this point that the Constitution insists that he must know the case against him.The justification for the deprivation of liberty cannot be treated as an internal document available only to the investigating agency. It must be communicated to the person whose liberty has been taken away so that he can contest the State's exercise of power. The right is therefore not about paperwork. It is about whether the person has any meaningful opportunity to resist the deprivation of his liberty.Why SC's Andrabi Verdict May Become a Turning Point for Bail Within UAPAIn Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol, the appellant was arrested in Punjab and produced before a Magistrate, but the investigating agency had failed to furnish him written grounds of arrest. The Magistrate consequently directed his release, holding that the arrest had been rendered illegal. The matter then reached the Supreme Court against the backdrop of the State's attempt to retain the ability to take the accused back into custody. The Court was therefore confronted with the more fundamental question of what value Article 22 has if the State can disregard it at the moment of arrest and then rely upon subsequent proceedings to keep the consequences of that violation from affecting custody. The Court's answer was clear: a subsequent remand order does not cure an unconstitutional arrest, and the later filing of a chargesheet or taking of cognizance cannot retrospectively validate a deprivation of liberty that was unconstitutional when it occurred.The Supreme Court expressly held that where Article 22(1) has been violated, the question of demonstrable prejudice does not arise. The constitutional guarantee itself has been breached. That approach is sound because requiring an arrested person to demonstrate additional harm would risk making the protection circular. The person was denied the very information necessary to challenge his arrest, and the law would then ask him to demonstrate how that denial affected his ability to challenge the arrest.Article 22 cannot be interpreted in a manner that makes its protection dependent upon the very opportunity that its violation has taken away. The Court therefore treated the safeguard as fundamental rather than merely procedural and made immediate release the consequence of its breach.This is also why release following an Article 22 violation rests on a prior and more fundamental conclusion: the custody itself cannot continue because the arrest did not satisfy the Constitution. That distinction prevents the State from converting a constitutional wrong into an ordinary bail dispute. If the police fail to comply with Article 22 and the person is nevertheless kept in custody because the allegations against him are serious, the constitutional guarantee becomes little more than an advisory instruction. The seriousness of the offence may justify a lawful arrest. As the Supreme Court put it, a person released for violation of Article 22(1) is not merely enlarged on bail; he is released from illegal and unconstitutional detention.Why an Allahabad HC Order Could Change How Police Use Preventive DetentionThe judgment ultimately reinforces that constitutional law sometimes forgets in the language of procedure: liberty is not protected merely by declaring rights. Rights become meaningful when courts attach consequences to their violation. Article 22 does not tell the police that it would be preferable to inform an arrested person of the grounds of arrest. It imposes a constitutional condition upon detention.The State may investigate, arrest and prosecute, but when it takes away a person's liberty, it must remain answerable for the manner in which it does so. If it cannot tell the person why he has been arrested, it cannot demand that he remain in custody while the State gets its constitutional obligations in order.The real significance of Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol lies in restoring some meaning to the words personal liberty. An arrest is the moment when the coercive power of the State is brought most directly against an individual, and it is precisely at that moment that constitutional safeguards must matter most. The State may have the power to arrest, but it does not have the power to keep a person in custody first and explain the basis of that custody later. Article 22(1) places a simple obligation on the State: tell the arrested person why he has been deprived of his liberty and give him the means to challenge it. When the State fails to do so, release is not an indulgence extended to an accused. It is the Constitution asserting that even in the pursuit of crime, there are limits beyond which the State cannot go. (Kumar Kartikeya is an advocate, Supreme Court of India. This is an opinion piece and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)
